A motor-controller bracket on an electric aircraft cracks eight hours into a twenty-hour vibration test. An engineer files the fix.

Now four people price that fix by hand: a cost engineer, a buyer, a planner and a cost accountant. In one study, a change like this waited a hundred and forty-four days, for about two and a half hours of real work.
Fern does that work in about a minute.
This is Bowman Aviation's change system. Jeff files ECR-0417. Fern reads the change, then the costs, suppliers and stock in Bowman's ERP, and posts its impact assessment right on the request.

Four hundred and fifteen dollars more per aircraft. A one-time cost of a hundred and forty-two to a hundred and fifty-six thousand. And the new bracket reaches the line thirteen weeks late, because the supplier quotes fourteen.
Code computes every number, and every number shows where it came from. The agent writes the words. A figure it cites must match the computed result to the digit, or Fern rejects the post.

Bowman's own rules decide what Fern may approve. A six hundred and twenty-two dollar panel change, it approves by itself. The bracket is over Bowman's hundred-and-fifty-thousand-dollar limit, so it goes to the board, with nine conditions.
Fern also sees how changes collide. Two open requests need the same magnet supplier. Qualify both in one lot, and Bowman saves about a hundred and eighty thousand dollars.
When the board approves, Fern drafts the new bills of materials and journal entries in the ERP. A named person submits every one.
Bowman is fictional. The ERP, the change system and the agents are real, and running.
Fern. The cost engineer, cost accountant and supply-chain analyst for every engineering change.
